newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA'S HANEKOM DEFENDS ACTION ON KWV WINE GROUP.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA'S HANEKOM DEFENDS ACTION ON KWV WINE GROUP.

text.p: South African Land and Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom on Monday defended his intervention in efforts by the KWV cooperative to become a private company, dismissing charges that he was trying to nationalise its assets.

The opposition National Party is among those who have accused Hanekom of a thinly disguised bid to nationalise the assets of the wine and brandy cooperative in his court action last month which delayed KWV's restructuring.
"Nothing could be further from the truth," Hanekom said in an editorial page article in Business Day newspaper.
"KWV chief executive Willem Barnard is on record as saying that he would not want in the newly formed company anything to which it was not entitled," Hanekom said.
Hanekom won a court application which has effectively put KWV's conversion into a company on hold until August, when the two sides will return to court.

KWV, the statutory regulator of South Africa's wine and spirit industry, had initially hoped to complete the conversion by the end of last month in a bid to compete more effectively in the 50 or so countries where it operates.

But Hanekom objected that further study was needed into whether KWV's assets belonged to its members or to the state, into how the industry would be regulated once KWV became a private company, and into the possibility that KWV would compete unfairly in the domestic market.
At its annual general meeting last month, KWV expressed determination to complete its conversion and insisted it would not part with members' assets.
Hanekom has appointed an auditor to probe the assets, which include large stocks of brandy accumulated over many years.

"I needed to ensure that the KWV's planned restructuring be put on hold until the implications relating to regulation, competition and the ownership of assets had been determined," the minister said on Monday.
"I am convinced that my interventions serve the best interests of the growers, producers, wholesalers, workers, consumers and future entrants in the wine industry as a whole," Hanekom said.
KWV had no immediate comment on his statement.
